svg.title: Hippocrates & Galen: The Four Humours and the Theory of Opposites
svg.desc: Educational museum diagram showing Hippocrates' Four Humours wheel (Blood: Spring, Air, Hot and Wet, Heart/Liver, Sanguine; Yellow Bile: Summer, Fire, Hot and Dry, Gallbladder, Choleric; Black Bile: Autumn, Earth, Cold and Dry, Spleen, Melancholic; Phlegm: Winter, Water, Cold and Wet, Brain/Lungs, Phlegmatic) alongside Galen's Theory of Opposites (Contraria Contrariis Curantur) clinical rebalancing examples.
svg.text: EDEXCEL GCSE HISTORY · CLASSICAL & MEDIEVAL AETIOLOGY (c.400 BC – c.1700)
Hippocrates & Galen: The Four Humours and the Theory of Opposites
PART I · HIPPOCRATES OF KOS (c.400 BC) — NATURALISTIC HUMORAL BALANCE
The Wheel of the Four Humours, Seasons, Elements & Qualities
PART II · CLAUDIUS GALEN (2ND CENTURY AD) — CLINICAL REBALANCING
Galen's Rule: Illness (dyskrasia) occurs when one humour becomes
excessive. Physicians restore balance by prescribing a remedy with the
exact opposite temperature & moisture — or evacuating excess fluid.
CLINICAL CASE 1 · WINTER CONGESTION & SHIVERING CHILLS
CLINICAL CASE 2 · SANGUINE BURNING FEVER & PLETHORA
WHY HUMORAL THEORY DOMINATED EUROPE UNTIL c.1700
1. Church Endorsement: Galen wrote that the body was designed by
one Creator — fitting Christian doctrine; Church-controlled universities
taught Galen's texts as infallible truth and discouraged human dissection.
2. Diagnostic Authority: Combining uroscopy wheels (urine colour,
smell & taste), zodiac charts and herbal materia medica gave trained
physicians a complete, rational-looking explanation for every illness.
GCSE SIGNIFICANCE: Hippocrates separated medicine from supernatural gods via clinical observation, while Galen locked the
humoral Theory of Opposites into a 1,500-year Church-backed orthodoxy that blocked germ pathology until the 19th century.
